procedural_history.originating_court: District & Sessions Judge (acting as Presiding Officer of the Special Court due to leave of absence)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders dated 1st March, 2017, 4th March, 2017, 7th March, 2017 and 14th March, 2017 (presumably from the Special Court and/or District & Sessions Judge) were challenged.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Appeal No.311/2017 and Criminal M. (Bail) No.525/2017 before the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi. The High Court rejected both the Criminal Appeal and the Bail Application on 22nd May, 2017.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court rejected his appeal and bail application. The Supreme Court was hearing Criminal Appeal Nos. 2181-2182 of 2017.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court was within its power to extend the judicial custody of the accused pending a decision on the application for extension of the period of investigation.

facts: The prosecution filed an application to extend the period for investigation on 28.02.2017, before the initial statutory period expired.
The accused filed an application for statutory (default) bail on 02.03.2017, after the prosecution's application was already submitted.
The court could not immediately decide on the prosecution's application, partly due to the designated judge being on leave.

While the prosecution's application was pending consideration, the court extended the accused's judicial custody on several occasions (from 01.03.2017 until 08.03.2017), when the charge-sheet was ultimately filed.
law: An accused's right to statutory or default bail does not become absolute if an application by the prosecution to extend the investigation period is already pending before the court.
The right to default bail can only be exercised if the prosecution's application for an extension of time is formally and expressly rejected by the court.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the lower court acted legally because the prosecution had filed its application for an extension of time before the initial period expired. There was no lapse on the part of the investigating officer.
The existence of this pending application provided a valid legal basis for the court to extend the accused's judicial custody while it considered the request.

Since the prosecution's application for extension was still under consideration and had not been rejected, the accused's right to default bail had not yet materialized. Therefore, the court was within its power to extend the judicial custody.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the lower court was within its power to extend the judicial custody of the accused because a valid application from the prosecution to extend the investigation period was already pending before it. This pending application superseded the accused's subsequent claim for default bail, rendering the continued custody legal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was entitled to statutory bail under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C.

facts: Before the 90-day period for filing the charge-sheet expired, the Additional Public Prosecutor filed an application on February 28, 2017, to extend the time for investigation.
After the 90-day period lapsed, the appellant filed an application for statutory bail on March 2, 2017.
At the time the appellant sought bail, the prosecutor's application for an extension of time was still pending and had not been decided by the court.
The charge-sheet was subsequently filed on March 8, 2017, while both the extension application and the bail application were still pending.
The Special Court ultimately rejected the appellant's statutory bail application on March 14, 2017.
law: An accused's right to statutory bail under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C. becomes an indefeasible right only if the charge-sheet is not filed within the prescribed period.
If the prosecution files a timely application to extend the period for investigation, the accused's right to statutory bail does not automatically accrue upon the expiry of the initial period.

The right to statutory bail in such a situation is merely an 'inchoate' (incomplete) right, which only becomes a full, enforceable right if the court formally and expressly rejects the prosecution's request for an extension of time.
application: The Court reasoned that since the prosecutor had already filed for an extension of time before the 90-day period expired, no indefeasible right to bail had accrued to the appellant when he filed his application on March 2, 2017.
The appellant's right was, at best, an 'inchoate right' that was contingent on the court's decision regarding the extension application.
The Court held that it could not have considered the appellant's bail application while the prosecutor's request for an extension was still pending.
The right to statutory bail would have 'ignited' only if the court had rejected the prosecutor's application. This did not happen.

By the time the matter was considered, the charge-sheet had already been filed on March 8, 2017. The filing of the charge-sheet extinguished any potential right to statutory bail, making the grant of such bail 'impermissible'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's appeal, holding that he was not entitled to statutory bail because his right had not become indefeasible. The prosecution's pending application for an extension of time prevented the right from accruing, and the subsequent filing of the charge-sheet extinguished this inchoate right entirely.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was entitled to statutory bail under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was entitled to statutory bail based on the legal precedents set in the cases of Uday Mohanlal Acharya v. State of Maharashtra and Sanjay Dutt v. State through CBI.
respondent_arguments: The precedents cited by the appellant (Uday Mohanlal Acharya, Nirala Yadav, and Sanjay Dutt) were not applicable as the legal principles in those cases were established in light of their specific facts.
The High Court was correct to consider the merits of the Public Prosecutor's report requesting an extension for the investigation, which was filed before the appellant applied for bail.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An accused's indefeasible right to statutory bail, which accrues if the investigation is not completed within the prescribed period, is only enforceable prior to the filing of the charge sheet (challan). This right is extinguished and ceases to be enforceable the moment the charge sheet is filed, if the accused has not already availed of it. Once the charge sheet is filed, any application for bail must be decided on its merits under the standard bail provisions, not under Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: If an accused files an application for statutory bail and the prosecution files a prayer for an extension of time to complete the investigation, both applications should be considered together.
In a situation where there is both an application for statutory bail and a request to extend the investigation period, bail cannot be granted unless the prayer for the extension of time is rejected.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The indefeasible right to statutory bail under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C. is enforceable only prior to the filing of a challan or a valid application for the extension of the investigation period. If an application for bail and a request for extension of time are both pending, they must be considered together, and bail can only be granted if the court first rejects the prosecution's request for an extension. The right to bail is extinguished if not availed of before the extension application is filed, and the custody of the accused during the pendency of such an application is not illegal.
legal_tests_applied: The 'Indefeasible Right' Test from Sanjay Dutt v. State through CBI: The indefeasible right to be released on bail accrues to the accused but it is enforceable only prior to the filing of the challan and does not survive or remain enforceable once the challan is filed, if not already availed of. The filing of an application for extension of the investigation period has the same effect as filing a challan in this context.

The 'Simultaneous Consideration' Test from Sanjay Dutt v. State through CBI: If an application by the accused for release on bail and a prayer from the prosecution for extension of time to complete the investigation are both pending, they should be considered together. No bail can be given unless the prayer for extension of the period is rejected.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's claimed 'indefeasible right' to statutory bail was not availed of before the Public Prosecutor filed a report seeking an extension of the investigation period. The filing of this report extinguished the appellant's absolute right to bail.

The precedents cited by the appellant, including Uday Mohanlal Acharya and Sanjay Dutt, were not applicable in his favor because, as per the principle laid down in Sanjay Dutt, the right to bail became contingent upon the court's decision on the prosecution's extension application, which was filed first.

The court found that the custody of the accused was not illegal while the application for extension of the investigation period was pending consideration, as the court was within its power to decide on that application.
why_respondent_won: The High Court was correct to consider the merits of the Public Prosecutor's report requesting an extension for the investigation, as it was filed before the appellant applied for bail.

The legal principle from the Constitution Bench in Sanjay Dutt's case dictates that the grant of statutory bail is subject to the refusal of a pending prayer for extension of the investigation period. Since the extension was warranted, the appellant was not entitled to bail.

The court explicitly stated, 'We are in full agreement with the said conclusion reached by the High Court,' affirming the respondent's position that the extension application must be decided on its merits before considering the bail application.
policy_considerations: To avoid further delay in a case involving personal liberty, the court found it undesirable to remit the matter back to the special court for a proper decision on the Public Prosecutor's report. Instead, the court decided to consider the report on its merits to secure the ends of justice and prevent abuse of process.
